title: Publish with GitHub Pages
intro: Turn an existing GitHub repository into a free public website. Complete Create a GitHub Repo first if you do not have files on GitHub yet. GitHub’s buttons change over time — focus on: Pages settings → public URL → commit updates.

steps.title: What GitHub Pages is
body: GitHub Pages serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other static files from a repository. It does not run server-side languages like PHP or a custom database on the Pages host.
That makes it perfect for portfolios, documentation, and learning projects — including this reference site. Your site gets a URL such as https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO/.

tips: Static means the server sends files as-is; interactivity still works with client-side JavaScript.
You can use a custom domain later if you want.

steps.title: Prerequisites
body: You need a GitHub account, a public repository, and at least an index.html file on the branch you will publish (usually main).
If you have not done that yet, follow the Create a GitHub Repo guide first, then return here.

steps.title: Enable GitHub Pages
body: Open your repository on GitHub → Settings → Pages (sometimes under “Code and automation”). GitHub’s settings layout changes — look for Pages.
Choose a publishing source (usually Deploy from a branch). Select the branch (main) and folder (/ root or /docs). Save. Wait a minute for the first deploy.

images.caption: Replace with a screenshot of Settings → Pages

tips: If you cannot find Pages, use the Settings search box.
Build status may appear as a green check on commits when using Actions-based Pages.

steps.title: Choose the publishing source
body: Common beginner choice: branch main, folder / (root). If you keep site files in a docs/ folder, select that.
Only one source is live. Commits on that branch update the site.

images.alt: Placeholder: branch and folder source options
images.caption: Replace with a screenshot of Deploy from a branch options

steps.title: Find your website URL
body: After enabling, Pages shows a URL like https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME/. Visit it.
If you see a 404, wait a minute, confirm index.html is at the published root, and hard-refresh. Project sites need the repo name in the path; assets should use relative URLs.

images.alt: Placeholder: Pages settings showing the public URL
images.caption: Replace with a screenshot of your Pages URL on the settings page

tips: For project Pages, prefer relative paths (./style.css) so assets resolve under the repo subpath.
mistakes: Expecting https://username.github.io without the repo name for a project repo.
Using absolute paths starting with / that ignore the project subpath.

steps.title: Update your website
body: Change a file locally or on github.com → commit to the publishing branch → wait for Pages to rebuild → refresh the live URL.
Caching can briefly show old assets — hard refresh if needed.

steps.title: Edit on GitHub vs Git locally
body: GitHub website editing is great for small text changes. Local Git (clone, branch, commit, push) scales better for real development and works with editors like Cursor or VS Code.
Learn the web flow first; add the Git CLI when you are ready.

images.alt: Placeholder: web editor vs local Git workflow
images.caption: Replace with screenshots comparing web edit and local push

tips: You do not need to master Git before publishing your first page.
When you learn Git: status → add → commit → push is the core loop.

steps.title: Fix common problems
body: 404 at site URL: Pages not enabled, wrong branch/folder, or missing index.html. Unstyled page: wrong CSS path. Old content: wait for deploy or hard refresh.
Forms that POST nowhere: Pages has no backend — use a form service or static-only UX. Check the Actions/Pages build log if available.

images.caption: Replace with a screenshot of a common error you want to demonstrate

tips: Open DevTools Network tab and look for red 404 files.
mistakes: Assuming a missing stylesheet means CSS is “broken” when the path 404s.

steps.title: Add a custom domain (optional)
body: Buy a domain from a registrar. In repo Pages settings, add your custom domain and follow GitHub’s DNS instructions (usually A/AAAA or CNAME records).
Enable HTTPS once DNS verifies. DNS changes can take time to propagate. Exact DNS screens differ by registrar — trust their docs plus GitHub’s current custom domain guide.

Keep the GitHub docs tab open while editing DNS — UIs change.
